If I rank w first, I am guaranteed to be tentatively accepted there initially due to my priority of 1. However, if I am rejected later by w because they filled all their spots with higher-ranked students (by their internal criteria, not my ranking), I will propose to my second choice. If my second choice is z, I have a chance of being accepted there because I have priority 2. If my second choice is y, I might be rejected due to its overall popularity, and then I propose to my third choice. If my third choice is x, I might be rejected there as well.

Given that I have high priority at w, I should rank it first. My next best option is z, where I have priority 2. Ranking z second gives me a reasonable chance of being matched to it if I am rejected from w. Ranking y third is strategic. Even though I like y more than x, it is likely to be very competitive. If I get rejected from w and z, there is a chance that y will still have spots open, and I have priority 1 at y. Finally, I place x last, as it's my least preferred option.

Therefore, my optimal ranking is w > z > y > x.
